accroche: Four years standing, head tilted back, on a scaffold he designed himself. The movies preferred him on his back.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1508, Pope Julius II entrusts Michelangelo with decorating the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. The artist is 33, thinks of himself first and foremost as a sculptor, and has never painted a fresco on this scale. The job will occupy him for four years, until 1512: an entire work to produce above his own head.

The image lodged in the collective memory, popularized by the Hollywood film *The Agony and the Ecstasy* (1965) and by the Irving Stone novel it was based on, shows a man lying on his back, brush stretched toward the ceiling. That image is wrong.

## A Scaffold Built for Standing

Michelangelo designs the structure that will carry him himself. Rather than resting on the floor, it rests in holes cut high in the chapel walls, below the line of the windows, which leaves the space underneath free so that religious services can continue during the work. On this suspended platform, Michelangelo works standing up, head tilted back and arms stretched overhead. Never lying down.

He himself leaves a trace of this posture. In the margin of a sonnet addressed to his friend the poet Giovanni da Pistoia, he draws a caricature of himself painting this way, body arched backward, one arm raised. The American art historian William E. Wallace, whose research in Italy in the 1980s was funded by a National Endowment for the Humanities fellowship, confirms this arrangement from period documents: the framework was designed by an architect friend and built by the carpenter Piero Basso. Wallace also shows that Michelangelo never worked alone on this project: a team of some 13 assistants grinds the colors, prepares the plaster, cleans the brushes, and itself paints some of the secondary elements (painted architecture, ornaments, certain background figures).

## What the Body Paid

Standing with your head tilted back for four years is anything but comfortable. Michelangelo himself describes this suffering in the same sonnet, written around 1509, when the project is not even halfway done: his beard points toward the sky, he feels the back of his skull resting on his nape, his loins have pushed into his belly. By 1510, he has to hold his documents at eye level in order to read them; ophthalmology researchers would later attribute this disturbance, which was temporary, to the long hours spent looking up.

The myth of the painter lying down is therefore not just an error of detail. It replaces a genuinely grueling physical performance, carried out standing on a scaffold of his own design, with the help of a team, by a solitary, motionless feat, more spectacular to film, but one that erases precisely what the sonnet lets us see: a body bending under the weight of the work, without ever lying down.

carte.punch: The movies showed him lying on his back. He painted standing, head tilted back, for four years.
carte.idee: The myth says Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel lying on his back. In reality he worked standing, on a scaffold of his own design, head tilted back, with the help of a team of 13 assistants.

quiz.question: How do we know today that Michelangelo painted standing up rather than lying on his back?
choix: A contract found in the Vatican describes the posture imposed on the artist
Michelangelo drew himself painting that way in the margin of a sonnet, and the drawing matches the structure of his scaffold
No painter of the time could have held a brush effectively while lying down
Chemical traces in the fresco show drips that are incompatible with a lying position
quiz.explication: Michelangelo drew a caricature of himself painting standing up, head tilted back, in the margin of the sonnet sent to Giovanni da Pistoia around 1509; historian William E. Wallace cross-checked this drawing against the documents describing the scaffold. No contract or chemical analysis is involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to William E. Wallace, how many assistants helped Michelangelo on the Sistine Chapel project?
choix: None: he worked entirely alone on the project
Two apprentices, only in charge of grinding the colors
A team of some 13 assistants, handling a variety of tasks
About 50 workers, as on a construction site
quiz_supplementaire.explication: William E. Wallace shows that Michelangelo never worked alone: a team of some 13 assistants ground the colors, prepared the plaster, cleaned the brushes, and painted secondary elements.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what happened to Michelangelo's eyesight starting in 1510?
choix: He had to hold his documents at eye level in order to read them
He went completely blind until the end of the project
He developed a cataract that required surgery
His vision improved after years spent with his head tilted up
quiz_supplementaire.explication: By 1510, Michelangelo has to hold his documents at eye level to read them; researchers would later attribute this disturbance, which was temporary, to the long hours spent looking up.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, how was the Sistine Chapel scaffold designed?
choix: It rested on the floor, on beams running across the whole nave
It rested in holes cut high in the walls, below the windows
It hung from the ceiling by ropes fixed to the beams
It stood on movable trestles shifted every day
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The scaffold rested in holes cut high in the chapel walls, below the line of the windows, which left the space underneath free so that religious services could continue.
